2.2 Finding the right device with lsblk
lists block devices so you can pick the right one to mount.
A hot-pluggable device (one you can plug in while the system runs, such as a USB drive) may get a different name each time. So check before you mount.
lists all block devices, or only the one you name.
Match by size. If you just added a 64 GB device with one partition,
is the one you want. Think of checking the size of the parcels on a shelf to find the one you just delivered.

A blank MOUNTPOINT means the device is not mounted yet.
Mount by UUID, because a device name can change but the UUID does not.
Linux may detect disks in a different order after you add or remove devices. That changes their names. A
(universally unique identifier) is a very long
number (digits 0-9 and letters a-f) stored inside the file system. It stays the same until you recreate the file system.

The desktop mounts for you, but you must still unmount before you unplug.

Shutdown and reboot unmount everything for you. First they write any
data (data kept for a while in memory) to the disk. For removable drives you must unmount yourself.
. There is no "n" after the "u". Give it the mount point. It works like closing a shop till at the end of the day. All waiting sales are written in the book before you lock up.
File system data is often cached in memory. If you unplug a removable drive without unmounting it, you can corrupt the data. Unmounting first writes the cached data to the drive.

2.6 When umount says target is busy
A file system cannot be unmounted while a process is still using it.
is a running program. If any process uses files under the mount point,
(the program that reads your commands) counts when its current working directory, the folder you are "in", is inside the mount point.

lists open files and the process using each one. Then you can wait for the process to finish, or send it a SIGTERM or SIGKILL signal (messages that ask a program to stop, or force it to stop). Or just leave the folder. Think of trying to lock a room while someone still stands in it.
A common reason is a Bash shell using the mount point as its current working directory. Use
. Only the last command changes anything: it detaches the file system.
COMMAND PID USER   FD   TYPE DEVICE SIZE/OFF NODE NAME

database, a ready-made list of files. The list is not updated live. So
